node.label: Edward Said
node.date_label: Orientalism 1978 · The Question of Palestine 1979 · Covering Islam 1981 · “Orientalism Reconsidered” 1985 · Culture and Imperialism 1993
node.description: A Palestinian-American literary critic whose Orientalism (1978) reads European writing on 'the Orient' as 'a Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient': a discourse in Foucault's sense, durable through what Gramsci called hegemony, though he held, 'unlike Michel Foucault', to 'the determining imprint of individual writers' and denied that the Orient was 'a creation with no corresponding reality'. The Question of Palestine (1979) examined 'Zionism from the Standpoint of Its Victims', Covering Islam (1981) took up American reporting on Islam, and 'Orientalism Reconsidered' (1985) traced Orientalism to historicism, including the 'science of world history'. Culture and Imperialism (1993) added what Orientalism had 'left out', resistance to empire, and proposed reading the metropolitan canon 'contrapuntally, with a simultaneous awareness both of the metropolitan history that is narrated and of those other histories against which (and together with which) the dominating discourse acts'. In period, Bernard Lewis charged him with 'very arbitrary decisions' of scope, and Said replied in their 1982 exchange that it was 'idiotic to say that Orientalism is a conspiracy'; Sadik al-'Azm called his account of Marx 'a travesty' (1981); and a 1996 review summarised feminist critics as holding that critics of Orientalism 'continue to write out gender'.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Edward W. Said (1935–2003); Orientalism (1978); The Question of Palestine (1979); Covering Islam (1981); “Orientalism Reconsidered” (Cultural Critique, 1985); foreword to Selected Subaltern Studies (1988); Culture and Imperialism (1993). Readings: Sadik Jalal al-'Azm, “Orientalism and Orientalism in Reverse” (1981); Bernard Lewis, “The Question of Orientalism” and the Said–Lewis exchange (New York Review of Books, 1982); Cheryl McEwan on Reina Lewis, Gendering Orientalism (1996). Later: Robert Irwin, Dangerous Knowledge (2006).
node.scope_note: A literary critic, not a historian; the entry is for a framework historians meet across fields. It rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: Orientalism in the 1978 Pantheon first edition (introduction pp. 1–28 in full; pp. 94, 153–156, 204 and 321 for passages used); The Question of Palestine (1980 Vintage reprint of the 1979 book; pp. 56–59 and 74–76); the Covering Islam introduction (p. ix); 'Orientalism Reconsidered' (1985) in full; the foreword to Selected Subaltern Studies (1988, pp. v–x) in full; and Culture and Imperialism (1993 Knopf first edition; introduction pp. xii–xiv and xxv, and pp. 41–42, 51, 66, 240–245, 251 and 278). Not read: 'Traveling Theory' (The World, the Text, and the Critic, 1983) and 'Foucault and the Imagination of Power' (1986), both lending-only or closed here; his critique of Foucault is taken from Culture and Imperialism, which cites the 1986 essay as 'my critique'. He is not presented as a founder: a 1992 critique calls his blend of themes 'virtually a paradigm for a new generation of historians and anthropologists' (O'Hanlon and Washbrook, first page only) and a 1996 review calls Orientalism 'undoubtedly' the inspiration behind critical interest in 'empire, knowledge and power' (McEwan); these are readers' judgements. Contested in period by Lewis (1982) and al-'Azm (1981), both read; James Clifford's review (History and Theory, 1980), Lata Mani and Ruth Frankenberg (Economy and Society, 1985), Dennis Porter (1983) and Aijaz Ahmad (1991–92) are recorded but were not read: Porter is known here from Said's 1985 reply, Ahmad from Robert Irwin's later account (2006), Reina Lewis (1996) from McEwan's review. No post-2000 work by Said is used; Irwin (2006) is a labelled later reading.

proposed_edges.relationship: Orientalism as discourse and as a style of domination: Western knowledge and representation of 'the Orient' read through knowledge and power, extended to contrapuntal reading of the metropolitan canon with empire (1978–93)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. Orientalism (New York: Pantheon, 1978, first edition; page images checked): 'The Orient was almost a European invention' (p. 1); Orientalism as 'a style of thought based upon an ontological and epistemological distinction made between "the Orient" and (most of the time) "the Occident"' (p. 2) and as 'a Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient' (p. 3). He qualifies it at once: 'it would be wrong to conclude that the Orient was essentially an idea, or a creation with no corresponding reality'; 'The relationship between Occident and Orient is a relationship of power, of domination, of varying degrees of a complex hegemony' (p. 5); and he leaves open 'how one can study other cultures and peoples from a libertarian, or a nonrepressive and nonmanipulative, perspective. But then one would have to rethink the whole complex problem of knowledge and power' (p. 24). Covering Islam (1981, introduction, p. ix): 'The underlying theme of Orientalism is the affiliation of knowledge with power.' 'Orientalism Reconsidered', Cultural Critique 1 (1985), read in full: the issues are 'the representation of other cultures, societies, histories; the relationship between power and knowledge' (p. 89); 'what for the most part got left out of Orientalism was precisely the very history that resisted its ideological as well as political encroachments' (p. 94); 'Orientalism is a praxis of the same sort, albeit in different territories, as male gender dominance, or patriarchy' (p. 103). Culture and Imperialism (New York: Knopf, 1993, first edition): 'What I left out of Orientalism was that response to Western dominance which culminated in the great movement of decolonization' (p. xii); 'we begin to reread it not univocally but contrapuntally, with a simultaneous awareness both of the metropolitan history that is narrated and of those other histories against which (and together with which) the dominating discourse acts' (p. 51); 'contrapuntal reading must take account of both processes, that of imperialism and that of resistance to it' (p. 66). In-period reception and criticism. Bernard Lewis, 'The Question of Orientalism', New York Review of Books, 24 June 1982 (web text, read in full, no page numbers): 'To prove this point, Mr. Said makes a number of very arbitrary decisions. His Orient is reduced to the Middle East, and his Middle East to a part of the Arab world'; 'a history of Arabic studies in Europe without the Germans makes as much sense as would a history of European music or philosophy with the same omission'; 'The most rigorous and penetrating critique of Orientalist scholarship has always been and will remain that of the Orientalists themselves.' Said's reply (NYRB, 12 August 1982): 'It is idiotic to say that Orientalism is a conspiracy or to suggest that "the West" is evil', while its 'modern discourse is correctly perceived as a discourse of power'; Lewis answered that 'It is difficult to argue with a scream of rage' and that the book 'takes a genuine problem of real importance, and reduces it to the level of political polemic and personal abuse'. Sadik Jalal al-'Azm, 'Orientalism and Orientalism in Reverse', Khamsin 8 (1981) (web text, read in full) credits 'laying bare Orientalism's persistent belief that there exists a radical ontological difference' between Orient and Occident, but holds that tracing Orientalism back to Homer 'simply lends strength to the essentialistic categories of "Orient" and "Occident"'. Rosalind O'Hanlon and David Washbrook (CSSH 1992; first-page extract only, as recorded in its source note) call Said's blend of themes 'virtually a paradigm for a new generation of historians and anthropologists' in Indian colonial history. Cheryl McEwan, Journal of Historical Geography 22 (1996), read in full: 'The inspiration behind the critical interest in empire, knowledge and power was undoubtedly Edward Said's groundbreaking and provocative Orientalism' (p. 489); feminist scholars 'argue that the critics of Orientalism and ethnocentric scholarship continue to write out gender' (p. 489); Reina Lewis's Gendering Orientalism (1996) is 'a response to Said in its efforts to destabilize the homogenizing tendencies of twentieth-century critiques of Orientalism' (p. 490). Said answered Dennis Porter's charge that he is 'ahistorical and inconsistent' as 'more weighty in assertion than it is in proof' (1985, p. 90); Porter's essay (1983) was not read. Not read: James Clifford's review essay (History and Theory 19, 1980) and Lata Mani and Ruth Frankenberg, 'The Challenge of Orientalism' (Economy and Society 14, 1985); both are recorded as metadata only. Later reading, labelled: Robert Irwin (2006, p. 299) writes that 'Early reviews of Orientalism were mostly hostile'. A contribution to postcolonial critique; the evidence does not make him its founder. edge_107 (language → post), edge_419 (post → indigenous) and edge_693 (post → geography) name him as a resource for others and stay.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: imperial_knowledge ('Imperial knowledge and cultural authority'; 'Texts acquire authority through institutions and citation; individual writers remain consequential'; works: Orientalism, 1978) holds him alone and matches the checked argument, including his insistence on individual authors (p. 23). The strand's works field could add Culture and Imperialism (1993) at release.

proposed_edges.relationship: Foucault's notion of discourse used to identify Orientalism, with an explicit disagreement over the weight of individual authors (1978)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. Orientalism (Pantheon, 1978; page images checked): 'I have found it useful here to employ Michel Foucault's notion of a discourse, as described by him in The Archaeology of Knowledge and in Discipline and Punish, to identify Orientalism. My contention is that without examining Orientalism as a discourse one cannot possibly understand the enormously systematic discipline by which European culture was able to manage—and even produce—the Orient politically, sociologically, militarily, ideologically, scientifically, and imaginatively during the post-Enlightenment period' (p. 3). 'Yet unlike Michel Foucault, to whose work I am greatly indebted, I do believe in the determining imprint of individual writers upon the otherwise anonymous collective body of texts constituting a discursive formation like Orientalism'; 'Foucault believes that in general the individual text or author counts for very little; empirically, in the case of Orientalism (and perhaps nowhere else) I find this not to be so' (p. 23). Elsewhere he writes of 'what Michel Foucault calls a discourse, whose material presence or weight, not the originality of a given author, is really responsible for the texts produced out of it' (p. 94), and he groups 'Gramsci, certainly, and Foucault and Raymond Williams in their very different ways' as illustrating that hegemonic culture's constraints on writers 'were productive, not unilaterally inhibiting' (p. 14). In-period criticism of the combination: al-'Azm (1981, read) objects that for Said 'representations, images, words, metaphors ... are, if not the very stuff of reality, then certainly much more important and informative substitutes for raw reality itself'. Later reading, labelled: Irwin (2006, pp. 289–290) sets the p. 23 and p. 94 passages against each other and argues that 'Foucault and Gramsci have different and contrasting notions of discourse'; Ahmad (1991–92) is reported by Irwin (p. 300) as finding that 'Said's allegiance to Foucault ... got him into the worst muddles'; Ahmad's texts were not read. The edge records Said's stated use and revision of Foucault, not a reading of Foucault's own position; Said's later criticism is edge 4.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The target is the new edward_said person entry, which has no strands.
proposed_edges.include_note: This edge tells the story of edge_024 (foucault → post, 'Said adopts Foucault’s discourse analysis while retaining individual authors’ effects'); see the proposed relabel of edge_024.

proposed_edges.relationship: Gramsci's hegemony and civil society used to explain the durability of Orientalism, and his 'inventory' of historical traces taken as the book's personal starting point (1978); consent for distant rule framed as 'a very Gramscian' question (1993)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. Orientalism (Pantheon, 1978; page images checked): 'Gramsci has made the useful analytic distinction between civil and political society'; culture works in civil society 'not through domination but by what Gramsci calls consent'; 'the form of this cultural leadership is what Gramsci has identified as hegemony, an indispensable concept for any understanding of cultural life in the industrial West. It is hegemony, or rather the result of cultural hegemony at work, that gives Orientalism the durability and the strength I have been speaking about so far' (pp. 6–7). Orientalism depends on 'this flexible positional superiority, which puts the Westerner in a whole series of possible relationships with the Orient without ever losing him the relative upper hand' (p. 7). 'In the Prison Notebooks Gramsci says: "The starting-point of critical elaboration is the consciousness of what one really is ..."'; Said notes that the English translation omits Gramsci's conclusion, 'therefore it is imperative at the outset to compile such an inventory', and calls his study 'an attempt to inventory the traces upon me, the Oriental subject' (p. 25). Culture and Imperialism (Knopf, 1993): 'The important point—a very Gramscian one—is how the national British, French, and American cultures maintained hegemony over the peripheries. How within them was consent gained and continuously consolidated for the distant rule of native peoples and territories?' (p. 51). In 1988 he described the Subaltern Studies scholars as influenced by 'many varieties of Western Marxism, Gramsci's most eminently' (foreword, Selected Subaltern Studies, p. x). Later reading, labelled: Irwin (2006, pp. 289–290) argues that 'Foucault and Gramsci had rather different ideas about the relationship between power and knowledge'. The edge records Said's stated use of Gramsci; it makes no claim about Gramsci's own Orient, which Said does not discuss in the pages read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Foucault criticised for discounting individual authors (1978) and for ignoring empire and dissolving the individual in a 'microphysics of power' that it is 'hopeless to resist' (1993)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. Orientalism (1978): 'Foucault believes that in general the individual text or author counts for very little; empirically, in the case of Orientalism (and perhaps nowhere else) I find this not to be so' (p. 23), while declaring himself 'greatly indebted' to Foucault (p. 23). Culture and Imperialism (Knopf, 1993): of Foucault and Raymond Williams, 'In the main I am in considerable sympathy with the genealogical discoveries of these two formidable scholars, and greatly indebted to them. Yet for both the imperial experience is quite irrelevant, a theoretical oversight that is the norm in Western cultural and scientific disciplines' (p. 41). Comparing Foucault and Fanon: 'Foucault's work moves further and further away from serious consideration of social wholes, focussing instead upon the individual as dissolved in an ineluctably advancing "microphysics of power" that it is hopeless to resist'; 'ignoring the imperial context of his own theories, Foucault seems actually to represent an irresistible colonizing movement that paradoxically fortifies the prestige of both the lonely individual scholar and the system that contains him'; Foucault 'swerves away from politics entirely' (p. 278). His note 198 refers the reader to 'my critique in "Foucault and the Imagination of Power"' (in David Hoy, ed., Foucault: A Critical Reader, 1986, pp. 149–155); that essay, and 'Traveling Theory' (1983), were not read. On p. 26 he also describes Foucault's turn to 'the local micro-physics of power that surround the individual'. Foucault's position is given only as Said presents it; no reply by Foucault was looked for. The critique is from a writer who kept using Foucault (edge 2); it is a disagreement within an acknowledged debt. edge_386 (post → foucault, Spivak and Stoler) records other postcolonial critics' engagements and stays.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The foucault person entry has no strands.

proposed_edges.relationship: Marx's 1853 writings on British rule in India read as an instance in which Orientalist generalisation overrode his sympathy for Asian suffering (1978), a reading contested in period as a travesty
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. Orientalism (Pantheon, 1978; page images checked), pp. 153–156. Marx 'identified the notion of an Asiatic economic system in his 1853 analyses of British rule in India, and then put beside that immediately the human depredation introduced into this system by English colonial interference, rapacity, and outright cruelty' (p. 153). After quoting Marx on England as 'the unconscious tool of history' and his Goethe citation: 'Marx's economic analyses are perfectly fitted thus to a standard Orientalist undertaking, even though Marx's humanity, his sympathy for the misery of people, are clearly engaged. Yet in the end it is the Romantic Orientalist vision that wins out' (p. 154); 'The idea of regenerating a fundamentally lifeless Asia is a piece of pure Romantic Orientalism' (p. 154); 'Marx is no exception. The collective Orient was easier for him to use in illustration of a theory than existential human identities' (p. 155); 'In part, of course, Marx was concerned with vindicating his own theses on socio-economic revolution' (p. 155); Marx is 'the case by which a non-Orientalist's human engagements were first dissolved, then usurped by Orientalist generalizations' (p. 156). The introduction announces it: 'The same kind of paradox is to be found in Marx, as I try to show in this book' (p. 14). In 1985 he names Marx among the historicists whose one human history 'either culminated in or was observed from the vantage point of Europe' ('Orientalism Reconsidered', p. 101). Marx's words appear here only as Said quotes them; the 1853 articles were not read. In-period counter-critique: al-'Azm (Khamsin 1981, read): 'I think that this account of Marx's views and analyses of highly complex historical processes and situations is a travesty'; 'only Said's excessive fascination with the verbal, textual and linguistic could lead him to portray Marx's mind as somehow usurped'; Marx's explanation 'testifies to his theoretical consistency in general, and to his keen realism'. Aijaz Ahmad's criticism of the same pages ('Between Orientalism and Historicism', Studies in History 1991; In Theory, 1992) is known here only from Irwin (2006, n. 32 to p. 296), who reports that Ahmad suggests 'Marx's position on rural Indians was not significantly different from his position on rural Germans'; Ahmad was not read. Later reading, labelled: Irwin (2006, pp. 295–296) calls the treatment a travesty and asks why there is no discussion of 'the Asiatic mode of production, Oriental despotism'.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: No strand (Sol 1.137 finding 8): no karl strand covers Marx's writings on colonial India; forces_relations_scope would be an approximate substitute.

proposed_edges.relationship: The named world-historical syntheses (Braudel, Wallerstein, Perry Anderson, Wolf) criticised as heir to Orientalist historicism: a homogenising scheme observed from a European vantage point that avoids its own relation to imperialism (1985); not a critique of every global or connected-history method
proposed_edges.map_label: Said's critique of named world-historical syntheses, 1985
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. 'Orientalism Reconsidered', Cultural Critique 1 (Autumn 1985), pp. 89–107, read in full (JSTOR copy). 'One of the legacies of Orientalism, and indeed one of its epistemological foundations, is historicism'; historicism 'meant that the one human history uniting humanity either culminated in or was observed from the vantage point of Europe, or the West'; out of the recuperation of what 'Eric Wolf has called people without history ... a still later disciplinary step was taken, the founding of the science of world history, whose major practitioners include Braudel, Wallerstein, Perry Anderson, and Wolf himself' (p. 101). He grants it 'greater capacity for dealing with ... the non-synchronous experiences of Europe's Other', but finds 'a fairly uniform avoidance of the relationship between European imperialism and these variously constituted, variously formed and articulated knowledges' (p. 101). 'The curious result is that the theories of accumulation on a world scale, or the capitalist world state, or lineages of absolutism depend (a) on the same displaced percipient and historicist observer who had been an Orientalist or colonial traveler three generations ago; (b) they depend also on a homogenizing and incorporating world historical scheme that assimilated non-synchronous developments, histories, cultures, and peoples to it'; 'the problem is once again historicism' (p. 102). He also rejects 're-cycling the old Marxist or world-historical rhetoric' (p. 103). In 1993 he contrasts revisionist works with 'the so-called world historians as well as the colonial Orientalists, who have tended to herd immense amounts of material under simple and all-encompassing rubrics' (Culture and Imperialism, pp. 41–42). The named historians' positions appear only as Said characterises them; no replies were looked for. The critique names practitioners mapped across several entries (Wolf on global; Wallerstein on dependency; Anderson on historicalsociology; Braudel's person entry); global is the target because he names 'the science of world history' as the object. edge_124 (post → global, Chakrabarty) stays.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: No strand (Sol 1.137 finding 8): Said names particular syntheses, not a strand's method.

proposed_edges.relationship: Foreword introducing Subaltern Studies to an Anglo-American readership, with his own caution that subaltern and elite histories are 'different but overlapping and curiously interdependent territories' (1988)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own in-period text. Foreword to Ranajit Guha and Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, eds., Selected Subaltern Studies (Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1988), pp. v–x, read in full (page images of a Digital Library of India scan, OCR checked against the images). He describes Guha's opening essay as 'fiercely theoretical and intellectually insurrectionary' (p. v) and the word subaltern as deriving 'from Gramsci's usage in the Prison Notebooks' (p. vi); 'rewriting Indian history today is an extension of the struggle between subaltern and elite' (p. vii). His addition: 'Yet even though his analysis is explicit on all the main issues, there is something that could perhaps be added to it here. And that is that no matter how one tried to extricate subaltern from elite histories, they are different but overlapping and curiously interdependent territories. This, I believe, is a crucial point. For if subaltern history is construed to be only a separatist enterprise ... then it runs the risk of just being a mirror opposite the writing whose tyranny it disputes' (p. viii). He places the group in 'the vast post-colonial cultural and critical effort' (p. ix) and calls its borrowing from Foucault 'the sharing of a paradigm, rather than slavish copying' (p. x); the volume is 'a crossing of boundaries, a smuggling of ideas across lines' (p. x). In 1985 he had already listed 'the group around Ranajit Guha (Subaltern Studies)' among anti-Orientalist projects ('Orientalism Reconsidered', pp. 104–105). A contribution of framing and reception to the series' Anglo-American appearance; it does not make him a member of the collective, a founder, or the source of its theory (the existing roster row says the same). edge_115 (subaltern → post) stays.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: No subaltern strand covers the series' reception or framing; popular_politics (Guha) is the strand his foreword discusses, but he is not part of it. A reviewer could add a reception strand.

proposed_edges.relationship: Culture and Imperialism's account of resistance culture: anticolonial histories such as James's The Black Jacobins and Antonius's The Arab Awakening read as a 'voyage in' to metropolitan culture, alongside post-independence critiques by Guha and Alatas (1993)
proposed_edges.map_label: Resistance culture and the voyage in, 1993
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own in-period text. Culture and Imperialism (Knopf, 1993), chapter 3, 'Resistance and Opposition'. He distinguishes liberal anti-colonialism, which did 'not dispute the fundamental superiority of Western man', from anti-imperialism, and argues 'there was no overall condemnation of imperialism until—and this is my point—after native uprisings were too far gone to be ignored or defeated' (pp. 240–241). Anti-imperialist work by writers from the peripheries in the metropolis is 'usually an extension into the metropolis of large-scale mass movements'; 'There is thus an overlap and interdependence that cannot theoretically be described as only the reactive assertion of a separate colonial or native identity'; 'The voyage in, then, constitutes an especially interesting variety of hybrid cultural work' (p. 244). He reads 'C.L.R. James's The Black Jacobins, published in 1938, and, appearing at almost the same time, George Antonius's The Arab Awakening' as works 'intended as serious works of scholarship and advocacy addressed from within a national movement for independence to a general audience', set against Ranajit Guha's A Rule of Property for Bengal (1963) and S. H. Alatas's The Myth of the Lazy Native (1977), which are 'post-colonial and specialist' (p. 245); 'history for Guha is critique, not the dutiful replication of colonialist objects, ideologies, and arguments' (p. 251). He also treats Fanon as one who 'programmatically seeks to treat colonial and metropolitan societies together' (p. 278). The introduction frames the chapter: 'What I left out of Orientalism was that response to Western dominance which culminated in the great movement of decolonization' (p. xii). Read: pp. xii, 240–245, 251, 278; the rest of the chapter (including the Fanon and Cabral sections) was not read closely. No in-period review assessing this chapter for historians was read. A contribution to how anticolonial histories are read and placed, not a claim that he wrote anticolonial history in their sense; The Question of Palestine (1979) is mentioned in the node, not used for this edge.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The chapter crosses several anticolonial strands: enslaved_revolution (James), colonial_subject (Fanon) and culture_liberation (Cabral). No single strand fits a reading of the tradition as a whole; null.
proposed_edges.include_note: The weakest of the eight edges: it rests on one book's chapter and has no in-period reception from historians. A reviewer may prefer to drop it, or to reverse it as an influence from clr_james (Said reads The Black Jacobins at length).

edges_considered_not_proposed.pair: edward_said → Orientalist scholarship (Bernard Lewis, H. A. R. Gibb, academic Orientalism)
edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: His central critique, in his own words (for example on Lewis, Orientalism, pp. 315–321, p. 321 read), targets academic Orientalism, which has no atlas entry. Lewis's reply (1982) and the exchange are recorded on edge 1 and in the node. If the atlas adds an Orientalist-scholarship or Middle East studies entry, a critique edge could be drafted from the pages listed here.

Culture and Imperialism (p. 278) calls Frankfurt School critical theory 'stunningly silent on racist theory, anti-imperialist resistance, and oppositional practice in the empire' and quotes Habermas's admission of 'a eurocentrically limited view'. It is a one-paragraph remark within the Foucault–Fanon comparison; folded into the record here. It could be drafted as a critique edge if reviewers want it.

'Orientalism Reconsidered' (1985, p. 94) contrasts Fabian with 'the standard disciplinary rationalizations and self-congratulatory cliches about hermeneutic circles offered by Clifford Geertz', and Said's 1982 NYRB letter calls Geertz's arguments against him 'rather trivial'. Geertz's NYRB review (1982) and 'Representing the Colonized: Anthropology's Interlocutors' (Critical Inquiry 1989; doi:10.1086/448481) were not read. Not proposed on a passing sentence.

Culture and Imperialism (p. 41) finds the imperial experience 'quite irrelevant' for Williams as for Foucault, while acknowledging a debt; Orientalism (p. 14) praises Williams. The Williams side is on the culturalstudies entry; the passage is recorded on edge 4 and not drawn as a second arrow.

The Question of Palestine (1979; 1980 reprint, pp. 75–76) places Zionist practice among 'the great dispossessing movements of modern European colonialism' and the declaring of lands 'open to European white settlers'. The settler_colonialism entry does not mention Palestine and no in-period bridge to that historiography was read; left for a reviewer.

His 1985 statement that Orientalism is 'a praxis of the same sort ... as male gender dominance, or patriarchy' (p. 103) is a concession to feminist criticism, not a contribution to gender history; the feminist critique is recorded on edge 1 (McEwan 1996, on Reina Lewis). Mani and Frankenberg (1985) were not read.
No evidence read. Chakrabarty's 1992 essay and Provincializing Europe are on the post entry beside Said; no passage connecting them was checked.

Said reads Fanon and James at length in Culture and Imperialism (pp. 245, 278); recorded on edge 8 rather than drawn as influences, since the pages read present them as subjects of his history of resistance culture.

proposed.relationship: Foucault's analyses of discourse, power and sexuality taken into colonial studies, and reworked there (1978–95)
proposed.evidence_note: Two uses on the post roster: Said's use of discourse in Orientalism (1978, p. 3; read 2026-10-14), and Ann Laura Stoler's Race and the Education of Desire: Foucault’s History of Sexuality and the Colonial Order of Things (1995), whose recorded verification (publisher description, not re-read) supports a 'critique of empire’s marginal place in Foucault and productive use of his 1976 lectures'. It does not claim that postcolonial history as a whole is Foucauldian; critical engagements are edge_386. Said's own use is the separate edge from his person entry.

proposed.relationship: Gramscian hegemony and consent in postcolonial accounts of cultural authority (1978–93)
proposed.evidence_note: Weak support for a group-level claim, so this revision is offered with the alternative below. Said's Orientalism (1978, pp. 6–7) and Culture and Imperialism (1993, p. 51) use hegemony and consent; his 1988 foreword (p. x, read 2026-10-14) describes the Subaltern Studies scholars, several of whom are also on the post roster (Chakrabarty, Chatterjee, Prakash, Spivak), as influenced by 'many varieties of Western Marxism, Gramsci's most eminently'. Gramsci's role in Subaltern Studies is edge_159. Said's own use is the separate edge from his person entry.

edge_385.alternative: Preferred if no second postcolonial user of hegemony is checked: leave edge_385 unchanged, accepting that it duplicates edge 3, or retire it at the rebuild.

new_sources.title: Edward W. Said, Orientalism (New York: Pantheon Books, 1978).
new_sources.citation: Edward W. Said, Orientalism (New York: Pantheon Books, 1978; first edition). Copy read: Internet Archive item orientalism-edward-said (file orientalism0000said_r4m0.pdf, scan of the Pantheon first edition).

verification.note: Page images and text layer of a scan of the Pantheon first edition (copyright page: 'Copyright © 1978 by Edward W. Said ... Published in the United States by Pantheon Books ... First Edition'). Running heads give book pages. Read: introduction pp. 1–28 in full; pp. 94, 153–156, 204 and 321. Passages used: 'The Orient was almost a European invention' (p. 1); 'a style of thought based upon an ontological and epistemological distinction' (p. 2); 'a Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient'; Foucault's 'notion of a discourse, as described by him in The Archaeology of Knowledge and in Discipline and Punish' (p. 3); 'a creation with no corresponding reality'; 'a complex hegemony' (p. 5); Gramsci's civil and political society, consent and hegemony, 'an indispensable concept'; 'flexible positional superiority' (pp. 6–7); 'The same kind of paradox is to be found in Marx'; 'Gramsci, certainly, and Foucault and Raymond Williams in their very different ways' (p. 14); 'unlike Michel Foucault, to whose work I am greatly indebted' and 'the determining imprint of individual writers' (p. 23); 'the whole complex problem of knowledge and power' (p. 24); the Gramscian 'inventory' (p. 25); 'what Michel Foucault calls a discourse, whose material presence or weight' (p. 94); Marx and India (pp. 153–156); 'every European ... was consequently a racist, an imperialist, and almost totally ethnocentric', with the following qualification (p. 204); Bernard Lewis (p. 321). Chapters 1–3 otherwise unread.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period text of the book, used for pages beyond the introduction transcription already in the graph (said_orientalism).

new_sources.title: Edward W. Said, The Question of Palestine (New York: Times Books, 1979; Vintage Books, 1980).
new_sources.citation: Edward W. Said, The Question of Palestine (New York: Times Books, 1979); copy read: First Vintage Books Edition, October 1980.

verification.note: Internet Archive item the-question-of-palestine-said-edward (OCR text layer of a scan; imprint: 'First Vintage Books Edition, October 1980 ... Originally published by Times Books ... in November 1979'). Pages are the 1980 Vintage reprint's; whether they match the 1979 Times Books edition was not checked. Read: contents; chapter 2 opening pp. 56–59; pp. 74–76. Passages used: chapter title 'Zionism from the Standpoint of Its Victims'; ideas to be examined 'genealogically' and 'as practical systems for accumulation (of power, land, ideological legitimacy) and displacement (of people, other ideas, prior legitimacy)' (p. 57); 'the great dispossessing movements of modern European colonialism' (p. 76) and lands declared 'open to European white settlers' (p. 76). The rest of the book is unread.

new_sources.scope_note: Node only (and the settler_colonialism note): the 1979 extension of his argument to Palestine.

new_sources.title: Edward W. Said, Covering Islam: How the Media and the Experts Determine How We See the Rest of the World (New York: Pantheon, 1981).
new_sources.citation: Edward W. Said, Covering Islam (New York: Pantheon Books, 1981).

verification.note: Internet Archive item covering-islam (ABBYY OCR of a scan without its imprint page). Its contents (Introduction ix; chapters on 'Islam as News', 'The Iran Story', 'Knowledge and Power'; Index 177) and an introduction that opens 'This is the third and last in a series of books', with no 1997 'Introduction to the Vintage Edition', match the 1981 edition; the publisher and edition are inferred, not seen. Only the introduction's first page was read. Passage used: 'The underlying theme of Orientalism is the affiliation of knowledge with power' (p. ix).

new_sources.scope_note: Node and edge 1: his own 1981 summary of Orientalism's theme.

new_sources.title: Edward W. Said, “Orientalism Reconsidered”, Cultural Critique 1 (Autumn 1985): 89–107.
new_sources.citation: Edward W. Said, “Orientalism Reconsidered”, Cultural Critique 1 (1985): 89–107.

verification.note: Read in full in a JSTOR PDF (cover sheet: Cultural Critique No. 1, Autumn 1985, pp. 89–107; stable URL 0882-4371(198523)0:1<89:OR>2.0.CO;2-6) available elsewhere. Crossref record for doi:10.2307/1354282 agrees (Cultural Critique, 1985, first page 89, author Said). Passages used: 'the relationship between power and knowledge' (p. 89); German Orientalism omission 'superficial or trivial'; Dennis Porter's charge 'ahistorical and inconsistent' and 'more weighty in assertion than it is in proof' (p. 90); 'the right of formerly un- or mis-represented human groups to speak for and represent themselves' (p. 91); 'got left out of Orientalism was precisely the very history that resisted'; Geertz's 'self-congratulatory cliches' (p. 94); historicism and 'the science of world history' (Braudel, Wallerstein, Perry Anderson, Wolf) (p. 101); 'theories of accumulation on a world scale ...' and 'the problem is once again historicism' (p. 102); 'a praxis of the same sort ... as male gender dominance, or patriarchy' (p. 103); Subaltern Studies, Spivak and Bhabha among anti-Orientalist projects (pp. 104–105).

new_sources.scope_note: In-period essay: his reply to critics and his critique of historicism and world history.

new_sources.title: Edward W. Said, Culture and Imperialism (New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1993).
new_sources.citation: Edward W. Said, Culture and Imperialism (New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1993; first edition).

verification.note: Internet Archive item cultureimperialism2 (file cultureimperiali00edwa.pdf; scan with running heads; imprint 'Copyright © 1993 by Edward W. Said ... Published in the United States by Alfred A. Knopf ... First Edition'). Read: introduction pp. xii–xiv and xxv; pp. 26, 41–42, 51, 66, 240–245, 251, 278 and note 198 (in the notes section). Passages used: 'What I left out of Orientalism' (p. xii); 'two historiographies, one linear and subsuming, the other contrapuntal and often nomadic' (p. xxv); Foucault and Williams, 'the imperial experience is quite irrelevant' (p. 41); 'so-called world historians' (p. 42); 'not univocally but contrapuntally'; 'a very Gramscian one' (p. 51); 'contrapuntal reading must take account of both processes' (p. 66); anti-colonialism and anti-imperialism (pp. 240–241); 'The voyage in' (p. 244); James, Antonius, Guha and Alatas (p. 245); 'history for Guha is critique' (p. 251); Foucault and Fanon, 'microphysics of power', 'swerves away from politics entirely', Frankfurt School silence (p. 278); n. 198 citing 'Foucault and the Imagination of Power' (1986) as 'my critique'. The rest of the book, including the Austen, Kipling, Camus and Verdi readings, is unread.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period book: contrapuntal reading, resistance culture, and his critique of Foucault.

new_sources.title: Sadik Jalal al-'Azm, “Orientalism and Orientalism in Reverse”, Khamsin 8 (1981): 5–26.
new_sources.citation: Sadik Jalal al-'Azm, “Orientalism and Orientalism in Reverse”, Khamsin: Journal of Revolutionary Socialists of the Middle East 8 (1981): 5–26.

verification.note: Read in full as web text on a website (no page numbers; the page introduces it as published in Khamsin in 1981). Volume and pages (8, 5–26) from Irwin (2006), n. 32, and a bibliographic listing; not seen on a page image. Passages used: Said's 'laying bare Orientalism's persistent belief that there exists a radical ontological difference'; tracing Orientalism to Homer 'simply lends strength to the essentialistic categories of "Orient" and "Occident"'; representations as 'much more important and informative substitutes for raw reality itself'; on Marx, 'I think that this account of Marx's views and analyses of highly complex historical processes and situations is a travesty', 'only Said's excessive fascination with the verbal, textual and linguistic', and Marx's 'theoretical consistency in general, and ... keen realism'. The web text may differ from the printed text in detail.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period Arab Marxist critique: sympathetic to the thesis, critical of its essentialism and its reading of Marx.

new_sources.title: Bernard Lewis, “The Question of Orientalism”, New York Review of Books (24 June 1982).
new_sources.citation: Bernard Lewis, “The Question of Orientalism”, The New York Review of Books, 24 June 1982.

verification.note: Read in full on the NYRB website (web text, no page numbers; volume and issue not recorded). Passages used: the term 'emptied of its previous content and given an entirely new one'; 'To prove this point, Mr. Said makes a number of very arbitrary decisions. His Orient is reduced to the Middle East, and his Middle East to a part of the Arab world'; the omission of the Germans; 'a remarkably arbitrary choice of works'; Said's attitude 'far more negative than that of the most arrogant European imperialist writers'; 'The most rigorous and penetrating critique of Orientalist scholarship has always been and will remain that of the Orientalists themselves.'

new_sources.scope_note: In-period critique by the leading Orientalist Said criticised.

new_sources.title: Edward W. Said, Oleg Grabar and Bernard Lewis, “Orientalism: An Exchange”, New York Review of Books (12 August 1982).
new_sources.citation: Edward W. Said and Oleg Grabar, letters, with a reply by Bernard Lewis, “Orientalism: An Exchange”, The New York Review of Books, 12 August 1982.

verification.note: Read in full on the NYRB website (web text, no page numbers). Passages used: Said, 'It is idiotic to say that Orientalism is a conspiracy or to suggest that "the West" is evil'; its 'modern discourse is correctly perceived as a discourse of power'; Geertz's 'rather trivial arguments against me'; the omission of German scholars explained. Lewis, 'It is difficult to argue with a scream of rage'; 'Mr. Said seems to be unable to conceive that there may be intellectual disagreements which are not political in origin or purpose'; 'The tragedy of Mr. Said’s Orientalism is that it takes a genuine problem of real importance, and reduces it to the level of political polemic and personal abuse.' Grabar's letter was not used.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period exchange: Said's reply to Lewis and Lewis's rejoinder.

said_orientalism.note: Re-read for the Said person entry (postcolonial batch). The PDF (57 pp.; title 'Said-Introduction and Chapter 1 of Orientalism') is a retyping of the Routledge & Kegan Paul 1978/1980 printing, which shares the Pantheon pagination (contents: Introduction 1, chapter 1 at 31, Notes 329). Its page breaks follow the book's, so book page = PDF page − 8: the earlier note's PDF pp. 11, 14–15 and 31–32 are book pp. 3, 6–7 and 23–24. Checked against the page images of the Pantheon first edition (pe137_said_orientalism_1978). The transcription has typing errors (for example 'employ is a Foucault’s notion'); quotations in the Said entry follow the scan.

said_subaltern_foreword_1988.note: Foreword read in full, pp. v–x, in page images of Selected Subaltern Studies (Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1988; title page 'Edited by Ranajit Guha and Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak') from the Digital Library of India scan on the Internet Archive (item dli.bengal.10689.12740), OCR checked against the images. Passages used: Guha's essay 'fiercely theoretical and intellectually insurrectionary' (p. v); subaltern from 'Gramsci's usage in the Prison Notebooks' (p. vi); 'an extension of the struggle between subaltern and elite' (p. vii); subaltern and elite histories as 'different but overlapping and curiously interdependent territories' and the risk of a 'separatist enterprise' becoming 'a mirror opposite' (p. viii); 'the vast post-colonial cultural and critical effort' (p. ix); influence of 'Western Marxism, Gramsci's most eminently', and of Foucault as 'the sharing of a paradigm, rather than slavish copying'; 'a crossing of boundaries, a smuggling of ideas across lines' (p. x). This edition is the Delhi printing; the New York OUP printing recorded in the original note was not compared.
